spotlight.name: Carnauba wax
spotlight.note: A wax from Brazilian palm leaves. It gives gummies their shine — and it's also a classic ingredient in car wax and shoe polish.

spotlight.name: Sorbitol
spotlight.note: A sugar alcohol that keeps the paste moist and sweet. It's the same sweetener found in sugar-free gum and candy.

spotlight.name: Sodium chloride
spotlight.note: That's plain table salt. Shampoo makers add it to make the liquid thicker.

spotlight.name: Lanolin
spotlight.note: A waxy grease that comes from sheep's wool. Sheep make it to waterproof their coats.

spotlight.name: Sodium citrate
spotlight.note: An emulsifying salt that makes slices melt perfectly smooth. With all the extras, many are legally labeled "cheese product," not cheese.

spotlight.name: Methylisothiazolinone
spotlight.note: A preservative that's a common skin allergen. The EU banned it from leave-on cosmetics, but it still shows up in rinse-off products and cleaners.

spotlight.name: Calcium disodium EDTA
spotlight.note: A preservative that grabs onto metals so flavors don't go stale. Doctors use the same compound to treat lead poisoning.

spotlight.name: Stearic acid
spotlight.note: A fatty acid from plant or animal fat. It's also what makes candles and bar soap hard.

spotlight.name: Polysorbate 60
spotlight.note: An emulsifier that keeps oil and water mixed. You'll find the same family of ingredients in lotions and creams.

spotlight.name: Isobutane and propane
spotlight.note: The same gases used in camping stoves. In a can, they're what puff the cream into foam.

spotlight.name: Nitrous oxide
spotlight.note: Also known as laughing gas — the same gas a dentist uses. It whips the cream as it leaves the can.

ingredients: Hydrogenated vegetable oil (coconut and palm kernel)

spotlight.name: Light cream
spotlight.note: It's sixth on the list. The tub is mostly water, oil and syrup — cream makes up only a tiny part.

spotlight.name: Cetearyl alcohol
spotlight.note: Despite the name, it's not drying like rubbing alcohol. It's a waxy "fatty alcohol" from coconut or palm that makes conditioner creamy.

spotlight.name: Phosphoric acid
spotlight.note: It gives cola its tang. It's also the main ingredient in many rust removers.

spotlight.name: Hydrochloric acid
spotlight.note: The same acid your stomach makes to digest food. Never mix it with bleach — together they release toxic gas.

spotlight.name: Alcohol (21.6%)
spotlight.note: That's about 43 proof — stronger than most wine. It's why the classic version burns.

spotlight.name: Glycerol ester of rosin
spotlight.note: Made from pine tree rosin. It keeps the flavor oils from floating to the top of the bottle.

spotlight.name: Ammonium hydroxide
spotlight.note: Ammonia dissolved in water — it's what cuts the streaks. Never mix it with bleach.

spotlight.name: BHT
spotlight.note: A preservative that stops fats from going rancid. The same antioxidant is also added to rubber, plastics and jet fuel.

spotlight.name: Red 40
spotlight.note: The same dye used in candy. Dogs don't care what color their treats are — the color is there for the humans.

spotlight.name: Defatted soy flour
spotlight.note: There's no bacon in them at all. They're crunchy bits of flavored, colored soy.

spotlight.name: Ethoxyquin
spotlight.note: A preservative first developed to stabilize rubber. The EU suspended it as an animal feed additive in 2017.

ingredients: Hydrogenated vegetable oil (coconut and/or palm kernel)

spotlight.name: Sodium caseinate
spotlight.note: A milk protein that keeps the oil blended into your coffee — even though the jar says "non-dairy." Labeling rules allow it.

spotlight.name: Zea mays (corn) starch
spotlight.note: The same cornstarch in your pantry, under its Latin name. Many brands switched to it from talc.

spotlight.name: Butane, isobutane, propane
spotlight.note: The first three ingredients are flammable fuel gases. Let it settle before you go near a curling iron or flame.

spotlight.name: Dimethyl silicone
spotlight.note: An anti-foaming silicone — the same family as the dimethicone in hair conditioner and lotion.

spotlight.name: Polyvinyl alcohol film
spotlight.note: The wrapper that dissolves in the wash. Pods look like candy, so keep them locked away from kids.

spotlight.name: Sodium bicarbonate + citric acid
spotlight.note: Baking soda plus acid — the same fizz as a science-fair volcano or a fizzy antacid tablet.

spotlight.name: Sodium aluminum sulfate
spotlight.note: The second-stage acid that makes "double-acting" powder rise again in the oven. Aluminum-free versions exist.

spotlight.name: Disodium inosinate & guanylate
spotlight.note: Flavor boosters that make MSG taste many times stronger. They're often made from yeast or fish.

spotlight.name: Magnesium sulfate
spotlight.note: Better known as Epsom salt. It's also sold as a laxative and as garden fertilizer.

spotlight.name: Taurine
spotlight.note: Named after bulls (Latin taurus) because it was first found in ox bile. Today it's made in a lab.

spotlight.name: Propylene glycol
spotlight.note: It keeps the syrup smooth. It's also the base of "pet-safer" antifreeze.

spotlight.name: Gum base
spotlight.note: A secret blend that can include synthetic rubber and polyvinyl acetate — a plastic also used in white wood glue.

spotlight.name: Cod liver oil
spotlight.note: Yes, fish oil — in a baby cream. It's there to soothe skin.

spotlight.name: Mechanically separated chicken
spotlight.note: A meat paste made by pressing chicken bones through a sieve under high pressure.

spotlight.name: Water sufficient for processing
spotlight.note: Pet food labels list water first when it's the biggest ingredient — the can is mostly water.

spotlight.name: Two corn syrups
spotlight.note: A common label trick: splitting the sweetener into two kinds pushes each one lower on the list.

spotlight.name: Ethyl alcohol
spotlight.note: The same alcohol found in drinks — denatured with bitter additives so nobody drinks it.

spotlight.name: PVP (polyvinylpyrrolidone)
spotlight.note: The hold in hair gel. It was used during World War II as a blood plasma substitute.

spotlight.name: Fruit pectin
spotlight.note: A natural gelling fiber from apple peels and citrus rinds. It's what turns juice into jelly.

spotlight.name: Sodium hydroxide
spotlight.note: Also called lye. It's the same chemical used to make soap — and to give soft pretzels their shiny brown crust.

spotlight.name: Optical brightener
spotlight.note: A dye that glows blue under UV light so white clothes look whiter. It doesn't clean anything — it just changes how fabric reflects light.

spotlight.name: Formic acid
spotlight.note: The same acid in ant stings. Its name comes from formica, Latin for ant.

spotlight.name: Sodium percarbonate
spotlight.note: Washing soda bonded with hydrogen peroxide. In water it releases oxygen bubbles — the "oxygen bleach" in stain removers.

spotlight.name: Limonene
spotlight.note: The compound that makes oranges smell like oranges. Indoors it can react with ozone in the air and form small amounts of formaldehyde.

spotlight.name: Calcium carbonate
spotlight.note: Basically ground-up chalk or limestone — the gritty scrubber. It's also the main ingredient in many antacid tablets.

spotlight.name: DMDM hydantoin
spotlight.note: A preservative that works by slowly releasing tiny amounts of formaldehyde.

spotlight.name: Ascorbic acid
spotlight.note: That's added vitamin C. It lets the box say "good source of vitamin C" even though it's mostly syrup and sugar.

spotlight.name: Paprika, turmeric and annatto
spotlight.note: Where the bright orange comes from. Many brands swapped artificial dyes like Yellow 5 and 6 for spices.

spotlight.name: Glucose syrup and sugar
spotlight.note: The first two ingredients. They taste like candy, which is exactly why the bottle has a child-proof cap.

spotlight.name: Concentrated juices
spotlight.note: Third on the list — after water and syrup. Many "juice drinks" are only about 10% juice.

spotlight.name: Sodium hydroxide
spotlight.note: Lye. It clears clogs by turning hair and grease into soap that rinses away. It can burn skin and eyes.

spotlight.name: Borax
spotlight.note: The sweet syrup is bait. Ants carry it home and share it, and the borax slowly works through the colony.

spotlight.name: Polyester sheet
spotlight.note: The sheet itself is plastic fabric. It's a carrier that melts softener and fragrance onto your clothes in the heat.

spotlight.name: Taurine
spotlight.note: Cats can't make enough of it on their own, so it's added — the same ingredient that's in energy drinks.

spotlight.name: Cocoa processed with alkali
spotlight.note: Also called Dutch-process cocoa. The alkali darkens the color and mellows the taste — and strips out much of cocoa's natural antioxidants.

spotlight.name: Dimethylpolysiloxane
spotlight.note: A silicone added to frying oil so it doesn't foam up. It's the same family of silicone used in caulk and conditioner.

spotlight.name: Carmine
spotlight.note: A bright red color made from crushed cochineal bugs. It's natural — but it's not vegetarian, and some people are allergic to it.

spotlight.name: Natural and artificial flavor
spotlight.note: There's no maple at all. "Table syrup" is corn syrup colored brown and flavored to taste like maple.

spotlight.name: Sugar and fructose
spotlight.note: Two kinds of sugar come first. The orange comes from flavoring and two synthetic dyes — not from oranges.

spotlight.name: Aluminum zirconium tetrachlorohydrex GLY
spotlight.note: An aluminum salt that forms tiny plugs in sweat ducts so you sweat less. Deodorant alone just covers the smell.

spotlight.name: Denatonium benzoate
spotlight.note: The most bitter chemical known. It's added so anyone who takes a sip — especially a child — spits it right out.

spotlight.name: Homosalate
spotlight.note: A chemical UV filter. The FDA has asked makers for more safety data, and Europe now limits how much can be used.

spotlight.name: Octylacrylamide/acrylates copolymer
spotlight.note: A plastic-like film that dries stiff on each hair. That's the "hold."

spotlight.name: Iron oxides
spotlight.note: Purified rust. Red, yellow and black iron oxides are mixed to match skin tones.

spotlight.name: Enzymes (protease, amylase)
spotlight.note: Proteins that break down stains the way your stomach breaks down food — protease eats grass and blood, amylase eats starch.

spotlight.name: Sodium hydroxide
spotlight.note: Lye. It turns baked-on grease into soap so it wipes away — and it can burn skin and eyes, so gloves on.

spotlight.name: Alkyl dimethyl benzyl ammonium chloride
spotlight.note: A "quat" disinfectant. It kills germs — and leaves a film behind, which is why labels say to rinse food surfaces.

spotlight.name: Dimethicone
spotlight.note: A silicone that leaves a glossy, slippery film — the same ingredient that makes hair conditioner feel smooth.

spotlight.name: Sodium tallowate
spotlight.note: Soap made from beef fat (tallow) mixed with lye. Old-fashioned soap has been made this way for centuries.

spotlight.name: Hydroxypropyl beta-cyclodextrin
spotlight.note: A ring-shaped sugar molecule made from corn starch. Odor molecules get trapped inside the ring — then fragrance covers the rest.

spotlight.name: Nonionic surfactant
spotlight.note: It makes water slide off dishes in a sheet instead of drying in spots. The label doesn't have to say exactly which one.

spotlight.name: Cocamidopropyl betaine
spotlight.note: A mild foaming agent from coconut oil — yet it was named "Allergen of the Year" in 2004 by the American Contact Dermatitis Society.

spotlight.name: Phenoxyethanol
spotlight.note: A preservative in many baby products. France advises against it in wipes and creams used on the diaper area of children under 3.

spotlight.name: Sodium fluoride
spotlight.note: It strengthens teeth, but kids shouldn't swallow it. That's why young children get just a rice-grain or pea-sized smear.

spotlight.name: Carrageenan
spotlight.note: A seaweed thickener that keeps the cocoa from sinking to the bottom. Scientists still debate its effect on the gut.

spotlight.name: Butylparaben
spotlight.note: A paraben preservative. The EU limits how much can be used in cosmetics and bans it in leave-on products for babies' diaper areas.

spotlight.name: Sodium laureth sulfate
spotlight.note: The foaming detergent that makes mountains of bubbles. Pediatricians warn long bubble baths can irritate young children's skin.

spotlight.name: Ethylene glycol
spotlight.note: It tastes sweet, which makes it dangerous to pets and kids. A bittering agent is added so it tastes awful.

spotlight.name: Methanol
spotlight.note: Wood alcohol. It keeps the fluid from freezing — and swallowing even a little can cause blindness.

spotlight.name: Paraffin wax
spotlight.note: A petroleum wax. When it burns, it gives off soot along with whatever is in the fragrance.

spotlight.name: Triethylene glycol
spotlight.note: Sprayed into the air to kill some airborne germs. It's also used to dry out natural gas in pipelines.

spotlight.name: Calcium chloride
spotlight.note: It actually heats up as it dissolves, so it melts ice fast. It can also dry out and crack pets' paws.

spotlight.name: Titanium dioxide
spotlight.note: The bright white in white paint — the same mineral used to whiten toothpaste and candy coatings.

statement: Most toilet paper starts out as trees.
explain: Most rolls are made from wood pulp, much of it from virgin forests. Bamboo and recycled paper are the main alternatives.

statement: Toilet paper is naturally white.
explain: Wood pulp is brown. Toilet paper is bleached to make it white — usually with chlorine dioxide.

statement: Scientists have found PFAS "forever chemicals" in toilet paper.
explain: A 2023 study tested toilet paper from around the world and found PFAS in it. PFAS can be used in paper-making.

statement: Recycled toilet paper can contain traces of BPA.
explain: BPA coats many thermal cash-register receipts. When receipts get recycled into paper, traces can carry over.

statement: "Flushable" wipes break down in pipes just like toilet paper.
explain: Toilet paper is made to fall apart in water within seconds. Wipes hold together, so they clog pipes and sewers.

statement: Toilet paper is designed to fall apart when it gets wet.
explain: Its fibers are short and only lightly bonded, so it breaks up in water instead of clogging your pipes.

statement: Packaged toilet paper has been sold in the US since the 1850s.
explain: Joseph Gayetty sold flat sheets of "medicated paper" in 1857. Rolls came a few decades later.

statement: Most people in the world use toilet paper.
explain: Much of the world — including large parts of Asia, the Middle East and southern Europe — mainly uses water instead.

statement: The average American uses more than 100 rolls of toilet paper a year.
explain: Estimates put it around 140 rolls per person per year — among the highest in the world.

statement: Brown, unbleached toilet paper is dirtier than white toilet paper.
explain: The color comes from skipping the bleach, not from dirt. Unbleached paper just skips a chemical step.

statement: Scented toilet paper can irritate sensitive skin.
explain: Added fragrance is one of the most common causes of skin irritation, and toilet paper touches very sensitive skin.

statement: The original 1891 toilet-roll patent drawing shows the paper hanging "over," not "under."
explain: Seth Wheeler's patent drawing shows the loose end hanging over the front of the roll. Debate settled?

statement: A 1930s toilet paper brand advertised itself as "splinter-free."
explain: Early paper could contain bits of wood. One brand made "splinter-free" a selling point in the 1930s.

statement: Most toilet paper sold in the US is made from recycled paper.
explain: Most US toilet paper is made from new (virgin) wood pulp. Recycled rolls are a small share of sales.

statement: Toilet paper sheets have gotten smaller over the years.
explain: Many brands have quietly shrunk sheet sizes and sheet counts while keeping the price the same.

statement: Bamboo toilet paper is always chemical-free.
explain: Bamboo still has to be pulped and is often bleached. Testers have even found PFAS markers in some bamboo brands.

statement: In March 2020, US toilet paper sales more than doubled in some weeks.
explain: Panic buying at the start of the pandemic sent sales soaring for weeks and emptied store shelves.

statement: "Two-ply" means two layers of paper pressed together.
explain: Each sheet is two thin layers bonded together, which makes it softer and stronger than one thick layer.

statement: Ancient Romans used a sponge on a stick instead of toilet paper.
explain: It was called a tersorium — a sea sponge on a stick, rinsed in water or vinegar and shared.

statement: Toilet paper companies must list the chemicals used to make it.
explain: There's no ingredient label on toilet paper. Makers don't have to disclose what goes into it.
